title: Plague Persists: Cases Still Reported in Africa and the US
title_zh: 鼠疫从未消失：非洲和美国每年仍有病例报告
lead: The plague, the bacterial infection that once wiped out tens of millions in medieval Europe, has never been eradicated. It remains a public health concern in parts of Africa and the rural American West, and is easily treatable with antibiotics if caught early.

paragraphs: The plague, the rare bacterial infection infamously known for killing tens of millions in 14th-century Europe, never went away. It is now easily treated with antibiotics. Since the 1990s, most human cases have been reported in Africa, especially Congo and Madagascar, according to the World Health Organization. There are an average of about seven human cases per year in the U.S., according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, mostly in rural areas of the American West.

A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia recently died of pneumonia, raising alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say testing showed no evidence of plague, but the research institute has been quarantined. "People think the plague is gone, it was something that occurred 500 years ago. It's not. It's here amongst us," said Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the U.K. "Unless you get rid of those wild animals, which of course is not possible, then you're not going to get rid of the bacteria."

Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague—also called the Black Death—are caused by the same bacteria, called Yersinia pestis. The bacteria spread naturally among rodents like prairie dogs and rats. Fleas that jump from infected animals and bite people can spread the disease. The bubonic plague is the most common form of the infection. It causes painfully swollen lymph nodes that are most commonly found in the groin, armpit and neck, called buboes. Other symptoms include sudden high fever and chills, headaches, and pain in the abdomen, legs and arms, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

There are two other forms of the plague: pneumonic plague, which can be caused by inhaling the bacteria, infects the lungs, while septicemic plague is an infection in the bloodstream. Both are fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization. Bubonic plague will often develop into the other two forms of plague if untreated. Other than bites from infected fleas, people can also get plague by touching infected bodily fluids, so health experts recommend taking extra care when handling dead or sick animals. The plague can also spread through the respiratory droplets of someone who has pneumonic plague.

When treated early with antibiotics, the plague can be cured. The key is to get to a doctor fast—otherwise the plague can be deadly. There is a vaccine, but the WHO only recommends it for people who are at high risk of infection, like laboratory and healthcare workers. There isn't strong evidence that vaccines can work against the pneumonic form. There's no plague vaccine available in the U.S.
paragraphs_zh: 鼠疫——这种因在14世纪欧洲夺去数千万人生命而臭名昭著的罕见细菌感染——从未消失。如今它很容易用抗生素治疗。据世界卫生组织称，自20世纪90年代以来，大多数人类病例报告于非洲，尤其是刚果和马达加斯加。据美国疾病控制与预防中心称，美国平均每年约有7例人类病例，主要分布在美国西部的农村地区。
西伯利亚一家鼠疫研究所的一名工作人员最近死于肺炎，在俄罗斯引起警觉，此前未经证实的媒体报道暗示她可能死于肺鼠疫。俄罗斯当局表示，检测未显示鼠疫证据，但该研究所已被隔离。英国雷丁大学的西蒙·克拉克说：“人们以为鼠疫已经消失了，是500年前才发生的事。但并非如此。它就在我们中间。”“除非你消灭那些野生动物，这当然不可能，否则你就无法摆脱这种细菌。”
肺鼠疫和更广为人知的腺鼠疫——也称为黑死病——由同一种细菌引起，这种细菌名为鼠疫耶尔森菌。这种细菌在草原犬鼠和老鼠等啮齿动物中自然传播。从受感染动物身上跳下并叮咬人类的跳蚤可以传播这种疾病。腺鼠疫是最常见的感染形式。它会导致淋巴结疼痛肿胀，最常见于腹股沟、腋窝和颈部，称为腹股沟淋巴结炎。据克利夫兰诊所称，其他症状包括突发高烧和寒战、头痛以及腹部、腿部和手臂疼痛。
鼠疫还有另外两种形式：肺鼠疫可由吸入细菌引起，感染肺部；而败血型鼠疫是血液感染。据世界卫生组织称，两者若不及时治疗都会致命。腺鼠疫若不治疗，往往会发展成另外两种鼠疫。除了受感染跳蚤的叮咬外，人们还可能通过接触受感染的体液感染鼠疫，因此卫生专家建议在处理死亡或患病动物时要格外小心。鼠疫也可以通过肺鼠疫患者的呼吸道飞沫传播。
若及早用抗生素治疗，鼠疫可以治愈。关键是要尽快就医——否则鼠疫可能致命。有疫苗，但世卫组织只建议高风险感染人群接种，如实验室和医护人员。没有强有力的证据表明疫苗能对抗肺鼠疫。美国没有可用的鼠疫疫苗。

Surprised to hear the plague is still around? Here's what to know.
Plague can attack lymph nodes, lungs and blood
People in Siberia have been dying of plague for at least 5,500 years. The earliest evidence of a form of the disease was
found in teeth from ancient hunter-gatherers
north of the region's Lake Baikal.
Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague—also called the Black Death—are caused by the same bacteria, called Yersinia pestis.

Bubonic plague will often develop into the other two forms of plague if untreated.
Plague can spread through fleas or bodily fluids
Other than bites from infected fleas, people can also get plague by touching infected bodily fluids, so health experts recommend taking extra care when handling dead or sick animals.
The plague can also spread through the respiratory droplets of someone who has pneumonic plague.
"If you cough, you can spread it to another person, but that doesn't travel very far," said Dr. Glenn Wortmann, MedStar Washington Hospital Center. "So you really need to be in face-to-face contact with that person to get pneumonic plague."
That's why "the chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen," he said.
Antibiotics can treat plague
The plague was never eradicated, but we've gotten better at preventing its spread and treating it in humans.
When treated early with antibiotics, the plague can be cured. The key is to get to a doctor fast—otherwise the plague can be deadly.
There is a vaccine, but the WHO only recommends it for people who are at high risk of infection, like laboratory and healthcare workers. There isn't strong evidence that vaccines can work against the pneumonic form.
There's no plague vaccine available in the U.S.
